metaDescription: Five cordless impact drivers at or under $150, from bare-tool Milwaukee and Ryobi to complete DEWALT kits, ranked by torque, motor type and battery value.
expertTake: The DEWALT DCF787D1 is the pick for most buyers because it arrives as a brushless driver with battery and charger, so there is nothing else to buy. The RYOBI ONE+ bare tool is the value pick if you already own 18V batteries, since 1,800 in-lbs is a lot of driver for a small outlay. Skip this bracket if you drive structural lag screws daily or need a battery platform that scales to tools above this price, because a bare driver is only as good as the packs behind it.
introParagraphs: An impact driver turns a motor's spin into rapid rotational hammer blows, which is why it drives long screws without cam-out and without twisting your wrist. At a modest budget the real decision is not torque but whether the box includes a battery, because a bare tool and a complete kit can sit at the same price and mean very different things.

This guide explains what torque numbers really measure, why motor type and battery size change daily use, and how to tell a bargain kit from a bare tool that costs more once packs are added. The picks are listed above, with reviews below. Listing prices move, and the cap reflects prices when this guide was updated.

products.name: DEWALT DCF787D1 20V MAX Brushless Impact Driver Kit
products.description:
A brushless motor replaces carbon brushes with electronic commutation, which cuts friction losses and lets the same battery drive more screws per charge. This kit pairs that motor with a compact body, so it fits between joists and inside cabinets where a longer driver will not. The LED stays on for 20 seconds after the trigger is released, which lights the screw you just drove and not a dark void.

Next to the CRAFTSMAN CMCF800 at 1,460 in-lbs, the DEWALT does not lead on advertised torque, and that is deliberate. The listing emphasizes runtime and durability over a headline number, and in practice 1/4 inch hex bits and deck screws are the limit of what most homeowners drive. If you plan to sink 6 inch lag screws daily, step up, but for decks, framing screws and cabinet installs it is enough.

Ownership is simple because the kit is complete. The battery and charger lock you into the 20V MAX platform, which is a wide family if you later add drills, saws and sanders. Keep the hex collet clean, store the battery cool and replace worn bits quickly, since a rounded bit tip causes cam-out long before the driver is worn.
products.bestFor: First-time buyers who want a complete brushless kit with no extra purchases.
pros: Brushless motor extends runtime and brush-free durability
Battery and charger included, so it works out of the box
Compact head reaches tight cabinet and joist spaces
20V MAX platform grows into a full tool line
cons: Advertised torque trails several competitors in this roundup
Single battery means downtime when it runs flat
No belt hook or bit holder details in the listing

products.name: RYOBI ONE+ 18V 1/4 Inch Impact Driver, 1,800 in-lbs (Tool Only)
products.description:
At 1,800 in-lbs this is the highest torque figure among the budget picks that do not require a premium platform. The impact rate of up to 3,400 per minute means the hammer and anvil strike often enough to keep a screw moving even when it bites into dense lumber. The bare tool listing is how it fits the cap: you get the driver and nothing else.

The catch is the battery. A ONE+ pack and charger are separate, and if you own none, the real outlay climbs above the DEWALT DCF787D1 kit. If you already own ONE+ batteries, though, this is the cheapest way to add serious driving power, and it works with the many tools in that family.

Ownership favors the existing RYOBI owner. The platform is broad and parts are easy to find, but a bare tool means you must keep track of battery health yourself. Charge packs before long jobs, and store them out of freezing garages.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who already own RYOBI ONE+ batteries and want strong torque cheaply.
pros: 1,800 in-lbs gives real driving power for the price tier
Impact rate of 3,400 per minute holds up in dense lumber
ONE+ platform works with a very wide tool family

products.name: Milwaukee 2953-20 18V 1/4 Inch Hex Impact Driver (Tool Only)
products.description:
At 2,000 in-lbs this driver tops the torque figures among the picks here, and it is built for people who drive screws all day. Single-handed bit insertion lets you swap bits while holding a board, which is a bigger time saver than it sounds when you change between a #2 Phillips and a driver bit for hundreds of fasteners.

Compared with the RYOBI at 1,800 in-lbs, the Milwaukee adds about 200 in-lbs and a platform built for jobsite abuse. It is a tool you buy once and run for years. The limitation is the same as the RYOBI: no battery in the box, so budget for M18 packs.

Ownership centers on the platform. M18 batteries power a large family of tools and will outlast most budget packs, which makes this a sound base for a long-term tool collection. Keep the hex collet free of debris, and give the tool a drop of oil in the collar every few months.
products.bestFor: Heavy users who already own or plan to build an M18 battery collection.

products.name: CRAFTSMAN CMCF800 20V MAX 1/4 Inch Impact Driver Kit
products.description:
With 1,460 in-lbs of torque and 2,800 RPM, this kit lands between the budget BLACK+DECKER and the 1,800 in-lbs RYOBI. The numbers are enough for deck screws and cabinet hardware, and the quick-release chuck allows one-handed bit changes. The LED light helps in dark corners and under sinks.

The tradeoff is brush technology. The listing does not mention a brushless motor, so expect the shorter runtime and brush wear of a conventional design. Next to the DEWALT DCF787D1, this model is the more affordable way into a complete kit, but it trades away the brushless efficiency.

Ownership favors light use. The kit includes a battery and charger, so there is no platform purchase to plan around. Brush-type motors will eventually need new brushes, so keep that in mind for heavy workloads.
products.bestFor: Weekend DIYers who want a complete kit with solid torque and a low outlay.

One-handed chuck release speeds bit changes
LED light lights up dark work areas
cons: No brushless motor mentioned, so runtime is shorter
Platform is narrower than DEWALT or Milwaukee
Impact rate is lower than the RYOBI at 3,400 per minute

products.name: BLACK+DECKER BDCI20C 20V MAX POWERCONNECT Impact Driver Kit
products.description:
This is the lightest-duty tool in the roundup, and the listing describes it as compact and light to reduce fatigue. The 1,375 in-lbs torque is the lowest among the kits, but it still covers drywall screws, small deck screws and furniture assembly. The 3,900 impact rate is the highest in the roundup, which gives the tool a quick, smooth feel when driving small fasteners.

It is not a tool for lag screws. The CRAFTSMAN CMCF800 offers about 85 more in-lbs, and the RYOBI offers about 425 more, so heavier work will stall it. For a household that drives a few dozen screws a month, that lower ceiling is a fair compromise for the cheapest complete kit.

Ownership is minimal. The battery and charger are included, but the POWERCONNECT platform is a narrow one, so adding tools later is less compelling than adding to DEWALT or RYOBI. Store the battery indoors and replace stripped bits promptly.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Torque is the twisting force the anvil delivers at peak, usually quoted in inch-pounds. For deck screws, 1,300 to 1,500 in-lbs is plenty, while lag screws and long structural fasteners want 1,800 or more. The BLACK+DECKER BDCI20C offers 1,375 in-lbs, the RYOBI 1,800 and the Milwaukee 2,000. Buyers often chase the highest number when the jobs they do never get past 1,400.

A bare tool leaves out the battery and charger, so the real price is higher unless you already own compatible packs. The DEWALT DCF787D1 and CRAFTSMAN CMCF800 arrive complete, while the RYOBI and Milwaukee do not. A complete kit is the safer choice for a first-time buyer. A bare tool only wins if you are already invested in that battery family.

Brushless motors avoid brush friction, which gives longer runtime and a longer service life. The DEWALT DCF787D1 is brushless, while the CRAFTSMAN and BLACK+DECKER listings do not say so. If you use an impact driver weekly, brushless matters. For monthly use, a brushed motor is a fine way to save.

Every battery family has its own tool range, and moving between them means rebuying packs. The Milwaukee M18 and DEWALT 20V MAX families are very broad, the RYOBI ONE+ is wide and economical, while the POWERCONNECT line is narrower. Choose the platform you want in five years, not the driver that is cheapest today.

Impacts per minute describe how often the hammer fires, and RPM is the spin speed. A higher impact rate gives smoother driving in small fasteners, while torque handles big ones. The BLACK+DECKER leads at 3,900 IPM, the RYOBI hits 3,400, and the CRAFTSMAN reaches 3,100.

A compact head reaches inside cabinets, between joists and under dashboards. One-handed bit changes, found on the Milwaukee and the CRAFTSMAN, save seconds on every swap. Heavier batteries add weight, so pick a compact pack if you work overhead.

specDecoder.meaning: This is the peak twisting force, measured at the anvil under ideal conditions. It indicates the largest fastener the driver can handle but not sustained performance.
specDecoder.watchFor: The Milwaukee's 2,000 in-lbs is a peak value, so expect lower torque under real load.

specDecoder.meaning: IPM counts hammer strikes per minute at no load. More impacts give a smoother feel in small screws.
specDecoder.watchFor: The BLACK+DECKER's 3,900 IPM does not mean it drives larger fasteners better than the RYOBI at 1,800 in-lbs.

specDecoder.meaning: RPM measures how fast the anvil spins before the hammer engages. It affects how quickly a screw seats in soft material.
specDecoder.watchFor: A 2,800 RPM CRAFTSMAN is not slower in practice than a 3,000 RPM BLACK+DECKER under load.

specDecoder.meaning: Tool only means the driver ships without a battery or charger. It makes sense only if you already own the platform.
specDecoder.watchFor: The RYOBI and Milwaukee listings are tool only, so add the cost of packs before comparing.

specDecoder.meaning: 20V MAX is a marketing rating for the peak voltage of a fresh battery, while nominal voltage is 18V. They are the same cell count.
specDecoder.watchFor: Do not assume a 20V MAX DEWALT is more powerful than an 18V Milwaukee on voltage alone.

howWeEvaluated.title: Torque against actual jobs
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared torque figures across the lineup and matched them to common fasteners. The Milwaukee at 2,000 in-lbs sits at the top, and the BLACK+DECKER at 1,375 sits at the bottom. We then judged whether the headline number matters for the work most buyers do.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit completeness
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked whether each listing includes a battery and charger, since that changes real cost. The DEWALT DCF787D1, CRAFTSMAN CMCF800 and BLACK+DECKER arrive complete. The RYOBI and Milwaukee do not.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor technology
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for brushless motors, which last longer and run longer on a charge. The DEWALT DCF787D1 states brushless, while others do not. Brushless was weighed more for frequent users.

howWeEvaluated.title: Platform value
howWeEvaluated.description: We assessed how broad each battery family is, from wide families like M18 and ONE+ to narrower ones. A tool that pairs with many others is worth more over time.

howWeEvaluated.title: Handling and features
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared weight, bit changes, LED lights and compact design. One-handed bit insertion and compact heads earned credit for daily use.

cards.label: Complete kit
cards.text: Battery and charger ship in the box, so the tool works the day it arrives. The DEWALT DCF787D1, CRAFTSMAN CMCF800 and BLACK+DECKER BDCI20C fall in this group.

cards.label: Bare tool
cards.text: You pay only for the driver, which makes sense if you already own the battery family. The RYOBI ONE+ and Milwaukee 2953-20 are bare tools, so check your pack inventory first.

howToChoose.note: Choose a kit if this is your first cordless tool; choose a bare tool only if the batteries are already on your shelf.

rows: M18 supports a very large tool range
20V MAX is broad and well stocked

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Deck screws need about 1,400 to 1,800 in-lbs and enough battery capacity to finish a board run. Check for a quick-release chuck, and choose a brushless motor if you are building a full deck.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The CRAFTSMAN CMCF800 handles standard deck screws at 1,460 in-lbs, while the RYOBI ONE+ at 1,800 in-lbs is better for long screws. The DEWALT DCF787D1 is the best fit for a full day of driving.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You drive structural screws daily or want a platform that grows. The Milwaukee 2953-20 at 2,000 in-lbs and the DEWALT DCF787D1 show where pro-grade ownership begins.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You assemble furniture and hang shelves a few times a month. The BLACK+DECKER BDCI20C or CRAFTSMAN CMCF800 will cover that and leave money for good bits.

maintenance.why: Sawdust and metal chips pack into the collet and stop bits from locking. A clogged collet also lets bits wobble and strip.
A worn bit slips under impact and strips screw heads. Impact-rated bits last longer than standard ones.
Lithium cells degrade fastest when stored full and hot. Keep them at about half charge in a cool room.

maintenance.interval: Every few months of heavy use
maintenance.why: A drop of light oil keeps the anvil spinning freely. Dry collars wear unevenly and add vibration.
Dirty contacts waste power and heat up the pack. Wipe them with a dry cloth.

faq.q: Should I buy an impact driver or a drill driver first?
faq.a: An impact driver is better at driving long screws without cam-out, while a drill driver is more versatile for drilling holes. Many owners eventually buy both. If you can only buy one for screws, an impact driver is the better pick.

faq.q: Is the cap enough for a good tool?
faq.a: Yes, as long as you pick the right package. A bare tool from a pro-grade platform offers more torque than a complete budget kit, but needs batteries. Listing prices move, so check the live cost.

faq.q: How long do these drivers last?
faq.a: Brushless models and pro-grade bare tools last longer under heavy use. Brushed models tend to last for years at weekend use. Battery packs usually wear out before the driver does.

faq.q: Does higher voltage mean more power?
faq.a: Not by itself. Torque, motor type and battery capacity decide real output. A 20V MAX label is a peak rating, and 18V tools share the same cell count.

faq.q: Can I use an impact driver as a drill?
faq.a: Only with hex-shank drill bits, and results are rougher than with a drill. The hammer action makes holes in wood messy. A drill driver is better for precise holes.
Yes. Standard bits can snap under impact because they are brittle. Impact-rated bits are made to flex and absorb the hammer blows.
